content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper, the authors propose an open-set semi-supervised learning (OSSL) method based on Visual Prompt Tuning, called OpenPrompt. Visual Prompt Tuning is a technique that has attracted much attention recently and aims to adapt a pre-trained model to a new unseen task by "fine-tuning" only a perturbation (prompt) added to the input data (e.g., image) while the backbone network is kept unchanged.


The proposed method learns the prompt to separate in-distribution (ID) samples from out-of-distribution (OOD) samples included in the unlabeled data. More specifically, it first finds a hypersphere (cluster) that covers most of the ID samples and uses its tangent lines to discriminate the ID and OOD samples, i.e., depending on whether a sample is inside or outside of the hypersphere. Then pseudo labels are assigned to the high-confident ID and OOD samples, and the prompts are learned to separate between ID and OOD samples in a contrastive learning manner.


Experiments are conducted by using various combinations of ID and OOD datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-30) and demonstrate that the method achieves comparable or better accuracy than existing OSSL methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[Strengths]

Summary: The proposed OSSL method is novel and interesting in its idea of using Visual Prompt Tuning. The method is potentially efficient. Thorough experimental results have been reported. 


+ Novelty:
OSSL is a new practical problem that has recently been proposed, and no existing studies using Visual Prompt Tuning have yet been reported. This paper is first to empirically demonstrate Visual Prompt Learning of OSSL is possible. The idea of learning prompts for ID and OOD samples in a contrastive manner is novel and interesting.


+ Potential Efficiency of Proposed Method:
Due to the nature of Visual Prompt Tuning that does not involve fine-tuning of the backbone network, the proposed method has the potential to perform more efficient learning than the existing OSSL methods.


+ Thorough Experiments:
Experiments have been conducted on a wide variety of datasets. Comparisons with existing methods as well as results of analysis on the main components and hyperparameters are reported.


========================================================

[Weaknesses]

Summary: I have several questions about the method design (which appears to be ad hoc), empirical effectiveness of the proposed method, and clarity of the method descriptions.


A. ID/OOD Binary Classification
Although the ID/OOD binary classification method given in Sec. 3.2.2 is simple, it seems somewhat ad hoc and is unclear if it is theoretically reasonable.
The binary classifiers for ID/OOD classifiers are initialized as tangent lines of a hypersphere covering all or most of the ID samples, and then the best line in terms of detected number of OOD samples is selected. However: 
- Why is the best classifier the one that detects the largest number of OOD samples?
- Is there any argument to show that this algorithm is valid or optimal? (e.g., the empirical risk measure is monotonically decreasing, etc.).
- This problem seems to be relevant to one-class classification, which has been well studied in the literature. Several major algorithms are available to solve this type of problems (e.g., 1-class SVM, kernel density estimation, etc.), why is it not acceptable to use one of them? How is the proposed method using tangent lines superior to these methods?


B. Technical Novelty of Method
Although the idea of learning prompts for ID and OOD samples in a contrastive learning manner is new and interesting, the method still largely relies on existing modern semi-supervised learning recipe, such as teacher-student model, EMA-based updating, consistency loss, and pseudo labeling with confidence-based thresholding. Prompt design also seems a minor update of the one originally proposed in Bahng et al. (2022).

C. Empirical Effectiveness
While the proposed method significantly reduces the number of trainable parameters, the accuracy gain of the proposed method over the existing methods is less than 1% in most of the experimental settings.

D. Clarity
The description of the cluster center in Sec. 3.2.2 is a little bit confusing to me. While saying "all ID samples form a cluster K," immediately after different cluster centers k_ic are prepared for each sample i=1,…,n.

E. Others
E-1. The threshold for ID/OOD classification is set at 0.1 in Eq. 5. Does this have impact on the final performance?

E-2. Just FYI, the idea of reusing OOD samples for OSSL has already been proposed in [1].
[1] Zhuo Huang, Jian Yang, Chen Gong. They are Not Completely Useless: Towards Recycling Transferable Unlabeled Data for Class-Mismatched Semi-Supervised Learning, IEEE TMM, 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* Novelty

Pros: This paper is the first to introduce Visual Prompt Tuning to OSSL, which I think the main novelty of this paper. 

Cons: Algorithmic novelty would be somewhat limited: although learning prompt in a contrastive learning manner is novel, most part of the algorithm largely relies on existing semi-supervised learning techniques.

* Clarity

Pros: The paper is mostly written clearly.

Cons: Some descriptions in Sec. 3.2.2 are a little confusing to me.

* Quality

Pros: Experiments are thoroughly conducted. 

Cons: The method seems ad hoc; no theoretical guarantee is presented. The accuracy improvement by the method is rather marginal (<1%). 


* Reproducibility

Pros: Key implementation details are given in the paper.

Cons: Codes is not submitted.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper is the first to introduce Visual Prompt Tuning to OSSL and may provide the community with a new direction in terms of introducing a new approach to OSSL. From the viewpoint of Visual Prompt Tuning, this paper is also valuable in demonstrating that prompt tuning is also effective for OSSL.


Although the proposed method does not clearly outperform the existing methods in terms of accuracy, it is valuable in that it significantly reduces the number of trainable parameters.


My main concern is that the algorithm is ad hoc and technically relies heavily on existing semi-supervised learning techniques, limiting its novelty. However, in light of the above contributions, I would say the paper is worth sharing.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a framework termed OpenPrompt for open-set semi-supervised learning (OSSL). Instead of fine-tuning the whole model learned from labeled data, OpenPrompt applies prompt learning techniques to propagate class information from labeled to unlabeled data. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance with much fewer learnable parameters.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
*** Strength ***
1. Open-set semi-supervised learning (OSSL) is an interesting task and the main challenge is how to leverage unlabeled data to strengthen the model trained from labeled data while factoring out the interference of out-of-distribution (OOD) samples. This paper provides an alternative to fine-tuning-based methods, which learns visual prompts to detect OOD data and enlarge the gap between ID and OOD samples. 
2. With less than 1% of trainable parameters compared to previous approaches, the proposed model shows competitive performance in the task of OSSL.
3. The proposed method achieves OOD detection without an additional outlier detector.

*** Weaknesses ***
1. The presentation of Section 3 is poor, making it hard to follow. In addition, some expressions and equations are not rigorous. For instance, how to obtain the cluster center of the ID samples in Equation 2? The loss described in Equation 11 only enlarges the gap between positive and negative samples, which should not be called a contrastive learning loss.
2. Based on my understanding, the major contribution of this paper is to introduce prompt learning techniques into OSSL. However, an important ablation is missing, where the visual encoder is fine-tuned instead of prompting and the rest parts of the framework remain the same. This could better demonstrate the advantages of prompting and supports the central claim of this paper.
3. Since prompt learning generally needs a strong pre-trained model, what is the performance of the proposed method when the labeled data is much less than the unlabeled ones?
4. It is not clear to me what is the difference between the proposed binary classifier updating method and the one suggested in [1]. It would be good if the authors could elaborate on this.
5. The claimed low computational cost is not well supported. 1) Although they deal with unlabeled data by only fine-tuning the prompt, they have to pre-train the whole network on the labeled data first. In contrast, previous works train the model using both labeled & unlabeled data only once (consequently the  #Paras in Table 1 is unfair). 2) There is no other strong evidence in the paper to demonstrate that the total computational cost of OpenPrompt is lower than in previous works.

[1] Exploiting a joint embedding space for generalized zero-shot semantic segmentation, ICCV 2021
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity and quality of this paper need significant improvement to meet the standard of ICLR. Prompting is a promising technique and introducing it to OSSL was not explored before to my knowledge. Hence, I believe there is some novelty to this work. It is hard to reproduce the results since plenty of details are missing. Detailed comments are in the following.

(1) The clarity of technical details and reproducibility:

- It is unclear that teacher and student networks are arranged respectively. It seems that only one network is learned at the pre-training stage. I conjecture that the pre-trained network is duplicated as teacher and student at the fine-tuning stage.
- as mentioned in the weakness part, it is unclear how the binary classifier $D(\cdot)$  is finally learned.  It seems that the  $N$ $D_j(\cdot)$ are only used temporally to calculate  parameters $d_1,d_2,k_{ic},k_{oc}$, while the $D_{ac}(\cdot)$ is the binary classifier that finally wanted.
- In Figure 4 (a). The ablation model w/o joint uses a discriminator as an OOD detector, as mentioned in Sec 4.3. But how this discriminator is designed and trained is not mentioned in the paper.

(2) Some concerns about the technical details:

- The CL loss between $v_{\phi}$ and $\bar{v_{\phi}}$ . In the fine-tuning stage, all unlabeled samples (including ID & OOD) are applied with $v_{\phi}$ , which indicates $v_{\phi}$ is not ID-specific. So is it make sense to apply contrastive loss between $v_{\phi}$ and the OOD-specific $\bar{v_{\phi}}$?
- The consistent loss in Eq.(10) might not be the optimal form. As the features $f_s, f_t$ obtained from the student and teacher network can be from IID or OOD domain, the distances should be viewed as a 2-d vector. Consequently the consistency is $\|d_1 - d_2 \|$, where $d_1 = [d(k_{ic},f_s),d(k_{oc},f_s)]$, and $d_2 = [d(k_{ic},f_t),d(k_{oc},f_t)]$. A simple 2-d example is $d_1 = [1,2], d_2 = [2,1], $ and $\|d_1 - d_2 \| \neq 0$, but when applying the form in Eq.(10), the $\mathcal{L}_C$ is 0.
- The number of parameters $2Cp(H+W-2p)$ mentioned in Sec.3.2.1 might not be correct. $C \times [(H+2p)(W+2p)-HW] = 2Cp(H+W+2p)$.

(4)  Problems with the experiments and other questions:

- As mentioned in the weaknesses part, the  #Paras in Table 1 is unfair. Because the proposed method has a pre-train stage which also needs the parameters of the ResNet. In contrast, previous works train the model using both labeled & unlabeled data only once. In addition, how is the #Paras 0.08 M calculated, given the p=40 and H=W=30 in CIFAR10? 2x30x40x(30+30+2x40)=33600.

- The threshold of selecting OOD samples is manually set as 0.1 in Eq.(5), and there are no ablation studies to demonstrate the effectiveness of different thresholds.

- Why the initial $D_j(\cdot)$ is selected by the largest OOD sample ratio $r_j$, i.e., Eq. (6) ?  What if this classifier is bad and it classifies many ID samples as OOD? In addition, is it truth that selecting $D_j(\cdot)$ by largest $r_j$ is equivalent to selecting the nearest $D_j(\cdot)$ ($1 < j\leq N)$ in the top-N furthest ones ?

- In Figure 4 (b) & (c), why the AUROC of 400 labeled samples per is worse than that of 50 & 100 labeled samples per class?
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents an interesting idea for OSSL by learning visual prompts. However, significant writing and presentation improvement is needed to help the readers to understand the paper. It would be great if there are more in-depth analyses about the advantages of prompt learning compared to fine-tuning in the task of OSSL.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This manuscript proposes OpenPrompt, which is a visual prompt-driven framework for handling open-set semi-supervised learning scenarios. Specifically, the proposed method reduces the number of parameters that need to be updated by adopting a concept of visual prompt, while pre-trained parameters are frozen. Under the prior semi-supervised loss objective and proposed OOD handling objectives (including detecting OOD method), the proposed method has shown its effectiveness in small-scale experiments such as CIFAR and ImageNet-30.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- Semi-supervised learning in the presence of unlabeled OOD samples is a practically important problem. 

Weaknesses
- Weak contributions; I think the proposed method has a trade-off between training costs and inference costs, at least no reduction in inference costs. To decide on a type of visual prompt, the proposed method must detect the ID- or OOD-ness of unlabeled samples, and then resent the unlabeled samples to the model to get its prediction at the inference time. I feel it is a weakness, not a strength. Moreover, the method (i.e., visual prompt) of reducing learnable parameters is taken from the existing method. 
- Marginal improvements; The experimental results in Table 1 are comparable to the baselines, but do not outperform them (within the standard deviation), even worse in some cases when more labels are available.
- Weak scalability; All experiments are performed on small-scale benchmarks, including ImageNet-30. Even though the proposed method has reduced the number of learnable parameters, the authors do not consider ImageNet-scale experiments, e.g., 1% or 10% ImageNet setups. Also, the number of given labeled samples is much larger than in conventional semi-supervised learning scenarios. For example, FixMatch also considered 4 labels per class are given, while the proposed method starts with 50 labels per class. 
- How accurate is the initial detection criterion at the beginning? (before fine-tuning stage)
- How are the effects of labeled samples on the proposed method? Does learning visual prompts still work when only a few labels are given? 
- How different are ID and OOD prompts? How big is it affecting the wrong prompt?

Minor comments
- Conflict between Figure 2 and Supervised loss (Section 3.3); Figure 2 demonstrates pseudo-label supervision from ID to OOD unlabeled samples, while Section 3.3 does from teacher to student. ("Therefore, we set the prediction results from student network as pseudo-labels")
- In Eq 10, there is no notation for differently augmented samples.
- In Eq 11, does cosine similarity loss mean cosine distance?
- typo; Fig. 4 (a), our model ... $\rightarrow$ Fig. 4 (b)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity
- There are several missing explanations, as I mentioned above. 

Quality
- There is a lack of analysis of scalability.

Novelty
- The proposed detection scheme is interesting.

Reproducibility
- I did not find any code implementations or many training details.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I recommend rejection for the following reasons; weak contributions, marginal improvements, and weak scalability, as I mentioned above.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors proposed a prompt-driven method for open-set semi-supervised learning. The proposed method consists of a smaller amount of learnable parameters added in the input space to help the rest of the frozen network to distinguish ID and OOD data. The authors proposed pre-training and then fine-tuning training stages and leveraged ID or OOD-specific learnable parameters during the fine-tuning stage. The main concept is that the authors used a small number of learnable parameters and demonstrate that they can be quite effective when distinguishing ID and OOD data (no classification accuracy is reported as far as I can tell). Overall, the paper is quite difficult to follow in my personal opinion.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Pros
- The authors provide method illustration and analysis to help the readers understand the proposed method.

## Cons
- The writing and presentation flow of the paper is unfortunately very difficult to follow. 
- The proposed method seems to be quite complicated compared to the existing approach
- The performance of the proposed method seems to be mainly from contrastive learning (from Table 1)
- The paper title and abstract were set out for open-set semi-supervised learning, but there is no classification accuracy or error rate on labeled data reported in the paper. Only the separation of ID and OOD AUROC performance is reported.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The abstract of the paper is a bit vague. It's not clear to me when the authors mentioned: (1) "suggest using a visual prompt-driven mechanism to obtain higher computational efficiency in the OSSL task". Without further context, it's hard to understand why a visual prompt-driven mechanism would provide higher computational efficiency. (2) "which can propagate class information from labeled to unlabeled data". It's vague when the authors use terms like class information. What kind of information about classes is being propagated? 
- The description of the proposed method in the introduction section is a bit hard to follow. I found myself still confused after reading through the introduction section and Fig. 1 a few times. I was not able to follow the proposed concept and grasp why would the proposed method work.
- Given that the proposed method requires two training stages (pre-training on labeled data and fine-tuning on unlabeled data), will the proposed method truly be more computationally efficient than the existing approach that learns online OOD detectors?
- In Sec. 3.1, teacher and student models should be denoted in Fig. 2 to help the readers understand what was described in Sec. 3.1. Without knowing for sure which one is the teacher and which one is the student, it's confusing when reading the paper.
- In Sec. 3.1, the authors mentioned feeding augmented unlabeled data to both teacher and student models but does not specify what the augmentations were. Does it follow the traditional way of feeding weak-augmented images to the teacher and strongly-augmented images to the student? However, the authors also mentioned that "pseudo labels received from the student network", does that mean the student network is used to generate pseudo-labels?
- In Sec. 3.1, the authors mentioned that the joint space takes feature as input and determines where the data belongs to ID or OOD samples. But, the authors do not state what exactly is "joint space". Was it a model or was it a heuristic approach to separate ID and OOD data?
- In Sec. 3.2.2, can the authors elaborate on why would learn a visual prompt in the pre-training stage propagate the class information of labeled data to unlabeled data in the fine-tuning stage?
- In Sec. 3.2.2, the authors form a cluster K using all ID (unlabeled) samples. But, how do we know if data belongs to ID or OOD? Without knowing which data is ID, how do the authors form cluster K? I assume that the authors meant to say that they form cluster K from labeled data (instead of ID unlabeled data).
- In Sec. 3.2.2, Eq. 4, what is D_j? Are they classifier candidates? In which, j-th represents j-th classifier? How would this number correspond to N (the top number of furthest data samples from the cluster)?
- The performance improvement shown in Table 1 seems to be within the STD of OpenMatch. This hinders the effectiveness of the proposed method. Especially when the contrastive learning part is removed from the proposed method, the performance seems to be lower than OpenMatch. Does that mean if we were to set up contrastive learning for OpenMatch, it will outperform the proposed method?

## Misc. 
- The citation format seems to be incorrect. The authors should use "\citep{}" instead of "\cite{}".
- "Open-set" should be used consistently throughout the paper (instead of "Open set").
- "OOD samples will be resent" --> "OOD samples will be re-send"
- What is Cp in Sec. 3.2.1? Was it C times p?
- I would suggest the authors not use "contrastive learning" as the naming of your loss in Eq. 11. This loss is quite different from what was commonly known as the contrastive loss that builds an embedding memory bank (Momentum Contrast for Unsupervised Visual Representation Learning).
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I was not able to follow and understand the core concept of the proposed method. The presentation flow and the writing of the paper are quite difficult to follow. I had to guess many parts of the proposed components in the paper (see some examples that I mentioned in the review under "Clarity, Quality, Novelty, And Reproducibility"). I would strongly suggest the authors carefully revise the paper and make sure the content presented is easy to follow.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
